exercises.title: Concurrency is throughput times latency
exercises.brief:
Write queue_depth_needed, returning how many requests must be outstanding to keep a device busy, given the operations per second it can complete and the microseconds each one takes.

Ask for fewer and the device is idle rather than slow.
exercises.concept: One relation decides how many requests you keep in flight, and it is not specific to storage.
hints: Multiply, and mind the units: the rate is per second and the latency is in microseconds.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. A million operations per second at a hundred microseconds each needs a hundred in flight, so the product has to be divided by a million to reconcile per-second with per-microsecond. Dividing rather than multiplying inverts the whole relationship.

exercises.after: Which is why a benchmark with one thread issuing one request at a time reports a tenth of a drive's capability and is not wrong about anything. It measured latency, correctly, and reported it as though it were throughput.

exercises.title: What the interface could express
exercises.brief:
Write achievable_ops, returning how many operations per second a device can actually deliver, given its capability, its latency, and the maximum number of commands the interface allows outstanding.

Thirty-two is enough for a device with one arm and nowhere near enough for one with dozens of chips.
exercises.concept: An interface that cannot hold enough requests outstanding limits the device regardless of what the medium could do.
hints: The interface caps the concurrency, and concurrency over latency is the rate.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. The device's own capability is a ceiling and the interface imposes another, so the answer is the smaller of the two: a queue of 32 at a hundred microseconds each cannot exceed 320000 a second whatever the medium can do.

exercises.after: A fast drive on the old interface was idle most of the time, waiting for a host that could not ask for enough at once. The bottleneck was not the medium, the controller or the wire, but the shape of the conversation, which is why the answer was a new interface rather than a faster one.

exercises.title: One queue, or one each
exercises.brief:
Write submit_cost, returning the cost of submitting a command, given whether the queue is shared between cores and how many cores are contending.

A shared queue needs a lock, and unit 026 priced a contended one.
exercises.concept: A queue per core has nothing shared, so submitting touches only memory that core already owns and the cost stops growing with the core count.
hints: With a private queue the core count does not appear in the answer at all.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. A private queue costs the same whether one core or sixty-four are submitting, because nothing is shared. A shared one costs the base plus a contention term that grows with the number of cores fighting for the line.

exercises.after: The depth was the headline and this is the design. Sixty-five thousand queues exists so that no two cores need ever touch the same memory to talk to the device, and it is the reason the per-command cost stopped rising as machines grew more cores.

exercises.title: Ringing once for several
exercises.brief:
Write doorbell_cost_per_command, returning the average cost of reaching the device per command, given the fixed cost of a doorbell write and how many commands are placed in the ring before ringing it.

The doorbell is the one part of the path that leaves the processor's own memory.
exercises.concept: The boundary is expensive, so cross it less often rather than more cheaply, which is the same move as the buffering in unit 022.
hints: The fixed cost is divided among the batch; the per-command cost is not.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Writing the command into the ring costs the same for every one, and only the doorbell is shared, so the average is the per-command cost plus the doorbell divided by the batch size. Dividing both understates it.

exercises.after: A driver that rings after every command is correct and slow. One that batches is correct and fast, and the difference is visible only under load, which is why it is the sort of thing that survives a review and shows up in a production graph.

exercises.title: Told, or asked
exercises.brief:
Write completion_overhead_ns, returning the host cost per completion under three schemes: 0 an interrupt each, 1 coalescing into batches, 2 polling.

Polling costs a core's time whether or not anything completed.
exercises.concept: The three trade the same quantity three ways, and the right choice depends on a rate the kernel cannot know.
hints: Coalescing divides the interrupt cost by the batch. Polling replaces it with the poll's own cost.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. Coalescing does not remove the interrupt, it shares one among several completions, so the per-completion cost is the interrupt divided by the batch. Polling removes it entirely and substitutes the cost of looking.

exercises.after: Polling wins when the completion rate is high enough that the core would have been busy anyway, and below that it is a core spent on nothing. Coalescing adds up to the timer's duration to every completion's latency, which is a good trade for a batch job and a bad one for a request somebody is waiting on.

exercises.title: Fixed per request, small per byte
exercises.brief:
Write cost_per_byte_ns, returning the average cost of moving a byte, given the fixed per-request cost and the transfer size at a given rate.

A command describes where the data is rather than containing it, so asking costs the same whatever the size.
exercises.concept: The per-request cost is fixed and the per-byte cost is small, which is why large requests are cheap per byte and small ones are not.
hints: Total time over total bytes, and the fixed cost is paid once per request rather than once per byte.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. The fixed cost is amortised over the whole transfer, so it divides by the byte count, and the transfer time per byte does not. Adding them without dividing the first reports the fixed cost as though every byte paid it.

exercises.after: A workload doing four-kilobyte reads spends most of its budget on bookkeeping, and the same bytes read in megabytes spends almost none. That arithmetic is the reason every layer in this part prefers large sequential requests, and it is the same reason unit 039's garbage collector does.

exercises.title: The scheduler that stopped earning its cost
exercises.brief:
Write reorder_benefit_ns, returning how much time reordering requests saves, given the seek time the reordering avoids and how many requests were reordered.

On a device with no seek time the benefit is zero and the work is not.
exercises.concept: A layer written to compensate for a constraint becomes overhead when the constraint disappears, and it takes a long time for anybody to notice.
hints: The saving is the avoided seeks; the cost of sorting is paid regardless.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees, and it will be the case with no seek time. Reordering saves the seeks it avoided, which on a device with none is nothing, and the sorting still costs what it costs. The answer can be negative, and that is the situation the whole block layer was rewritten over.

exercises.after: The best scheduler for a device with no seek time turned out to be barely a scheduler. The replacement gives each core a software queue and defaults to doing almost nothing, and the layer it replaced was not wrong, it had just stopped earning its cost.

exercises.title: Where the limit actually is
exercises.brief:
Write delivered_ops, returning how many operations per second a system delivers, given the device's capability and the host's software cost per operation in microseconds.

At a million operations per second the software becomes the limit.
exercises.concept: The bottleneck moved from the medium to the interface and then to the operating system, and each move made the previous layer's cleverness redundant.
hints: One core can perform only so many operations if each costs a fixed amount of its time.

diagnose.prose: A check disagrees. The host's rate is a million microseconds per second divided by the cost of one operation, and the answer is whichever of that and the device is smaller. Reporting the device's capability ignores the half of the system that is now the constraint.

exercises.after: A drive capable of a million operations per second behind a stack costing five microseconds each delivers two hundred thousand, and every one of those five microseconds is software. That is why io_uring exists, why polling exists, and why some workloads drive the device from userspace entirely.
